# Introduction

Climate change is having profound effects on Pacific salmon populations throughout their range, contributing to the declines of many stocks while introducing greater variability and uncertainty into assessments and planning. Although the significance of climate change for Pacific salmon is well established, its effects have been and will continue to be variable for the 5 species, 69 stock management units (SMUs) and over 450 conservations units (CUs) of Pacific salmon in Canada. The salmonscape of the future will be different than the past, with serious implications for the people, societies, and ecosystems of which salmon are an integral part.

A wealth of scientific research informs our understanding of future changes to freshwater and marine ecosystems, and how Pacific salmon are likely to respond to those changes [@crozier2023]. While many of the mechanisms of climate change vulnerability are understood, at least a conceptual level, there are few broad-scale assessments that evaluate the relative or absolute climate vulnerability of Pacific salmon across multiple species and wide geographic areas (e.g. Crozier et al. 2019). This gap is particularly notable across the Canadian distribution of Pacific salmon, which spans from the southern to the northern half of their range and includes a great diversity of life history types and ecosystems.

Climate change vulnerability assessments (CCVAs) can help bridge the gap between our scientific understanding and application towards resource management decisions and planning. Pacific salmon are a vitally important species, resource, and symbol within Canada, and in recent years have been the target of hundreds of millions of dollars in investments to support stock rebuilding, habitat restoration, fisheries monitoring, and hatchery enhancement. The success of these activities will be influenced by climate changes, which may lead to further declines in productivity for some stocks or outweigh the positive influences of rebuilding work. While there are many factors to be considered in prioritizing investments and making resource management decisions for Pacific salmon, assessment frameworks that are scientifically robust, transparent, and reproducible are more likely to be trusted and facilitate the incorporation of climate change considerations into decision-making [@boyce2022; @rangwala2021].

In this report, we present an indicator-based approach for assessing climate change risk factors across the Pacific salmon life-cycle. The framework incorporates recently developed, downscaled climate models in marine and freshwater domains [@weller2024; @peña2024], cumulative habitat stressors models [@murray2024], population status assessments [@csas2024], life history timing [@wilson2025], and environmental niche models [@iacarella2023] into 17 quantitative indicators. The indicators are grounded in ecological theory and represent biological mechanisms of climate change responses, including demographics, physiology, and genetic adaptation [@urban2016; @pacifici2015; @boyce2022].

We apply the climate vulnerability indicators for salmon (CVIS) framework to 5 species and 50 CUs of Pacific salmon within the Fraser River basin, an area of high life history diversity with variation in recent responses to climate change. Climate change is recognized as a prime threat to many populations within the Fraser basin, particularly for Fraser River sockeye and Interior Fraser Chinook, however, to date most assessments considering climate vulnerability have focused on specific CUs, species, or watersheds [@doutaz2023; @dionne2023]. Furthermore, many threats assessments and other attempts to evaluate climate vulnerability have been centered around expert judgement and categorical traits, limiting comparability across assessments.

By quantifying multiple mechanisms of climate vulnerability across a large basin, we aim to better understand differences in climate change risk at the individual CU, species, and basin level. In particular, we investigate which CUs are most likely to be at risk from climate change during their freshwater rearing, upstream migration, and nearshore marine life stages, and which factors are most important in differentiating that risk among CUs and species. We also quantify the sensitivity of risk rankings across different time periods (mid-century versus end-of-century), emissions scenarios, global climate models, and scoring frameworks to understand the influence of different methods and objectives for assessment. Ultimately, our framework provides a means for identifying patterns of climate change vulnerability across spatial areas and demographic units, and testing the sensitivity of those patterns to different models and assumptions to help identify the drivers of climate vulnerability.

# Methods Overview

The CVIS framework consists of 17 quantitative indicators (Table 1) classified into five categories based on mechanism and life-stage: freshwater spawning and rearing, upstream migration, nearshore marine, demographics, and genetics. Every indicator uses a quantitative metric, such as the mean stream temperature or percent change in flow, to represent risk. The indicator approach allows for flexibility in inputs and metrics of risk; various model types can be used to derive statistical summaries of risk depending on the mechanism to assess. Variation and uncertainty in indicator values are represented using 80% quantile ranges of global climate models where relevant.

```{r}

tbl_ind_report %>%
  arrange(Category) %>%               # ensure groups are contiguous
  gt(groupname_col = "Category") %>%  # turn Category into row-group headers
  # Make the header (column labels) bold
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(weight = "bold", align = "center"),
    locations = cells_column_labels()
  ) %>%
  # Center the row-group headers
  tab_style(
    style = cell_text(align = "center"),
    locations = cells_row_groups()
  ) %>%
  tab_options(
    table.font.size = "small",
    data_row.padding = px(1),
    row_group.padding = px(2),
    row_group.border.top.color = "gray75",
    row_group.border.bottom.color = "gray75"
  )



```

The framework focuses on CUs of Pacific salmon as the assessment unit. As the unit of biodiversity for Pacific salmon in Canada, CUs represent groupings based on life history characteristics, freshwater and marine adaptive zones, and genetic structure [@Holtby2007]. The number of populations and spatial distribution of CUs is variable, with some CUs representing just a single population with fewer than a thousand spawners per year while other CUs include dozens of populations and millions of spawners per year on average. Despite this variability, conservation at the CU level is critical for maintaining biodiversity under the Wild Salmon Policy, and the CU is an important unit for assessment that is used to determine aggregate stock status [@csas2024].

**Indicator Standardization**\
All indicators are standardized using response functions to translate raw values to a scale from 0 to 1, where 0 represents lowest risk and 1 is the highest risk relative to other CUs. Standardization facilitates easier interpretation and comparison of indicators, and allows the representation of risk based on stressor-response relationships and thresholds [@boyce2022]. Where relevant and defensible, physiological or ecological thresholds, such as optimal temperature limits, are used to parameterize standardization functions. This allows risk scores to be zeroed for environmental changes and other factors in situations where they are likely to remain within safe limits or have a positive influence on productivity.

**Overall Vulnerability Scoring**

Individual indicators represent a single mechanism or metric of climate vulnerability, but overall vulnerability is determined by the cumulative effects of multiple mechanisms and stressors that act within and across life stages. We apply multiple scoring methods for overall vulnerability to explore different causal relationships and interactions among individual indicators and categories. Comparing among scoring methods allows us to evaluate how relationships among indicators, weighting of indicators, and weighting of categories affect the relative vulnerability rankings among CUs. We summarize results and variation across four scoring methods that each reflect different assumptions for determining overall vulnerability.

**Emissions scenarios and time period**\
CCVAs can assess vulnerability for a particular time period or multiple time periods, as well as different emissions scenarios depending upon assessment objectives [@foden2013]. Our indicators that evaluate environmental change are based primarily on the CMIP5 suite of global climate models and results are presented focusing on the mid-century period under representative concentration pathway (RCP) 4.5, representing moderate emission reductions compared to business as usual. The influence of different emissions scenarios and time periods are assessed by evaluating changes in relative vulnerability rankings across RCP 4.5 and 8.5, and for mid-century (2041-2060) versus end-of-century (2081-2100) time periods.

# Freshwater Spawning to Rearing

#### Data Sources

**BCFishPass** - Freshwater fish habitat accessibility model used to subset accessible streams. [<https://smnorris.github.io/bcfishpass/index.html>]\
**CU boundaries** - spatial boundaries for CUs based on Freshwater Adaptive Zones. Taken from PSF data library [<https://data.salmonwatersheds.ca/result?datasetid=104>] **Cumulative Threats** - Cumulative threats to anadromous salmon stream habitat in the Fraser Basin [<https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/csas-sccs/Publications/SAR-AS/2024/2024_041-eng.pdf>]\
**Thermalscapes Stream Temperatures** - Statistically downscaled projections of August stream temperature developed across British Columbia [<https://datadryad.org/dataset/doi:10.5061/dryad.bzkh189fk>]

**Environmental Niche Models** - Models of current and future habitat favourability for British Columbia and the Western US [<https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/10.1139/cjfas-2023-0096>]

**PCIC Variable Infiltration Capacity With Glaciers (VIC-GL) gridded model** - Dynamically downscaled projections of stream temperature and flow from 1980 to 2099 for gauged watersheds within British Columbia [<https://pacificclimate.org/analysis-tools/salmon-climate-impacts-portal>]

**PSF CU-Specific Life History Timing** - timing of life history events for determining freshwater residency time [<https://datadryad.org/dataset/doi:10.5061/dryad.wm37pvmwx>]

**August flow projections at gauge stations** - Preliminary model outputs of statistically downscaled flow projections for gauge stations in British Columbia. Developed by Sacha Ruzzante et al.

#### Methods

Vulnerability indicators for freshwater spawning and rearing life stages represent environmental change to streams, as well as cumulative threats to stream habitats and freshwater residency times. The British Columbia Freshwater Atlas was used as the stream network with spatial delineation to Pacific salmon conservation units based upon conservation unit boundaries. The stream network was limited to accessible streams with channel width and gradients that meet criteria for intrinsic habitat potential for each Pacific salmon species using the [BC Fishpass accessibility model](https://smnorris.github.io/bcfishpass/02_model_access.html) and [habitat model](https://smnorris.github.io/bcfishpass/03_model_habitat_linear.html). For sockeye salmon, the habitat model also includes criteria for proximity to lakes. This filtering process removed smaller and inaccessible streams while retaining all stream segments with observed occurrences and modelled habitat potential.

Environmental change indicators included projected August stream temperatures, rate of change in August stream temperature, percent change in August flows, percent change in flows from November to January, and change in environmental niche model habitat suitability. Each indicator was calculated as the mean value across all stream segments assigned to the conservation unit, weighted by stream segment length. Temperature indicators (projected and rate of change) were based on a statistical downscaling approach fitted to streams throughout British Columbia [@weller2024]. Hydrologic indicators were based on the Pacific Climate Impacts Consortium gridded hydrological model that was further downscaled to the Fraser basin stream network [@iacarella2025]. For the indicator of percent change in August flows, an alternative set of projections using a statistical downscaling approach fitted to hydrometric stations in BC (Ruzzante in prep) was also applied to compare variation in responses (to be further described in an appendix).

Variation in environmental change indicators for each CU was summarized across global climate model projections and spatial dimensions using 80% quantile ranges. Spatial variation quantiles were weighted by stream length and characterized the range in responses for accessible streams with intrinsic habitat potential using the ensemble mean of climate model projections. Global climate model quantiles represented the variation of the weighted mean for streams within the CU boundary across all included global climate models (generally 6).

### i. Projected August stream temperature (tw8proj) {.tabset .tabset-pills}

**Metric:** The average of August stream temperatures across all years of the projection period (2041-2060 or 2081-2100) over all accessible streams with modelled habitat potential contained in the conservation unit (CU) boundary. Streams are weighted by stream segment length when calculating the average value. Projections from representative concentration pathways (RCP) 4.5 and 8.5 are included with an ensemble mean calculated from six global climate models.

For additional description of indicator see [A.1 Projected August stream temperature (tw8proj)](#a1.-projected-august-stream-temperature-tw8proj)

```{r projT plots}
# fw_indicators <- tbl_indicators$abbrev[tbl_indicators$type %in% c("fwR")]

for (rcp_pick in rcp_vec)
{
  cat("#### ", rcp_pick, "\n\n", sep = "")

  filter_std <- report_dat %>%
    filter(
      rcp == rcp_pick,
      period_code == default_period
    )

  make_indicator_plots(filter_std,
    ind_pick = "tw8proj"
  )

  cat("\n\n")
}
```

### ii. Rate of change in August temperature (tw8rate) {.tabset .tabset-pills}

**Metric:** The decadal rate of increase in August mean stream temperature from a baseline period of 1981-2000 to the projection period (2041-2060 or 2081-2100) averaged over all accessible streams with modelled habitat potential contained in the CU boundary. Streams are weighted by stream segment length when calculating the average value. Projections from RCP 4.5 and 8.5 are included with an ensemble mean calculated from six global climate models.

For additional description of indicator see [A.2 Rate of increase in August stream temperature (tw8rate)](#a.2-rate-of-increase-in-august-stream-temperature-tw8rate)

### iii. Proportional decrease in August flows (lowQpdelta) {.tabset .tabset-pills}

**Metric:** The change in average August flow from a baseline period of 1981-2010 to the projection period (2041-2060 or 2081-2100), expressed as a proportion of the average historical flow and averaged over all accessible streams with modelled habitat potential contained in the CU boundary. Streams are weighted by stream segment length when calculating the average value. Projections from RCP 4.5 and 8.5 are included with an ensemble mean calculated from six global climate models.

For additional description of indicator see [A.3 Proportional decrease in August flows (lowQpdelta)](#a.3-proportional-decrease-in-august-flows-lowqpdelta)

```{r}

```

### iv. Proportional increase in November to January flows (highQpdelta) {.tabset .tabset-pills}

Metric: The change in average flow for the months of November, December and January from a baseline period of 1981-2010 to the projection period (2041-2060 or 2081-2100), expressed as a proportion of the average historical flow and averaged over all accessible streams with modelled habitat potential contained in the CU boundary. Streams are weighted by stream segment length when calculating the average value. Projections from RCP 4.5 and 8.5 are included with an ensemble mean calculated from six global climate models.

For additional description of indicator see [A.4 Proportional increase in November to January flows (highQpdelta)](#a.4-proportional-increase-in-november-to-january-flows-highqpdelta)

### v. Ecological Niche Model change in habitat favourability (favchange) {.tabset .tabset-pills}

**Metric:** The change in habitat favourability from the baseline period (1981-2000) to the projection period (2041-2060 or 2081-2100), calculated as the difference between future and baseline favourability values and averaged over all accessible streams within the CU boundary. Habitat favourability is derived from environmental niche models (ENMs) fitted to salmon occurrence data and environmental predictors, providing a metric of environmental suitability that ranges from 0 to 1. The future favourability values use an ensemble mean of six GCMs from RCP 4.5 and 8.5 scenarios for the environmental predictors.

For additional description of indicator see [A.5 Ecological Niche Model change in habitat favourability (favchange)](#a.5-ecological-niche-model-change-in-habitat-favourability-favchange)

```{r}

      dsmodel %in% dsmodel_baseline
    )

  make_indicator_plots(filter_std,
    ind_pick = "favchange",
    spatial_pal_dir = 1
  )

  cat("\n\n")
}
```

### vi. Cumulative threats to stream habitat (CT)

**Metric:** A composite index of threats from human activity to stream habitat, calculated using a normalized additive model that combines nine threat categories including flow alteration, in-stream habitat destruction, riparian disturbance, nutrients, pollution, and sedimentation. The indicator is calculated as the mean cumulative threat score across all accessible streams with modelled habitat potential in the CU boundary, weighted by stream segment length.

For additional description of indicator see [A.6 Cumulative threats to stream habitat (ct)](#a.6-cumulative-threats-to-stream-habitat-ct)

```{r}

make_indicator_plots(report_dat,
  ind_pick = "cthr"
)
```

### vii. Freshwater residency time

**Metric:** The duration in days that juvenile salmon reside in freshwater from the start of egg incubation to ocean entry. For each CU, residency time is calculated using as the number of days from peak spawn timing to peak ocean entry timing, plus the typical number of years spent in freshwater (0 or 1).

For additional description of indicator see [A.7 Freshwater residency time (fwres)](#a.7-freshwater-residency-time-fwres)

```{r}

make_indicator_plots(report_dat,
  ind_pick = "fwres",
  make_spatial = F
)
```

# Upstream Migration

#### Data Sources

**PCIC Variable Infiltration Capacity With Glaciers (VIC-GL) gridded model** - Dynamically downscaled projections of stream temperature and flow from 1980 to 2099 for gauged watersheds within British Columbia [<https://pacificclimate.org/analysis-tools/salmon-climate-impacts-portal>]\
**PSF CU-Specific Life History Timing** - timing of freshwater life history events for each CU used for run timing and spawn timing [<https://datadryad.org/dataset/doi:10.5061/dryad.wm37pvmwx>]

**NUSEDS (New Spawning Escapement Database)** - CU spawning sites used to determine migration end points [<https://open.canada.ca/data/en/dataset/c48669a3-045b-400d-b730-48aafe8c5ee6>]

#### Methods

Indicators for the upstream migration life stage represent changes to stream temperatures and flows, and distance to spawning sites. For each CU, a migration path from river mouth to each NUSEDS spawning sites was created using the BC Freshwater Atlas stream network. Migration distance for each path was calculated as the length of all stream segments from river mouth to spawning site, and averaged across all NuSEDS sites to get an average migration distance for each CU.

To estimate temperatures and flow during upstream migration, an upstream movement model was applied to stream segments within the migration path and used to subset days of the year and spatial grid cells from the VIC-GL model. The model began with stream segments within 100km of the river mouth at the start of run timing. The front end of this spatial subset was moved upstream at a rate equal to the distance to spawning sites divided by the number of days between spawn timing start and run timing start. This assumes that the spawn timing start coincides with arrival to the spawning sites. The tail end of the migration was modelled to arrive at the spawning grounds at the peak spawn date, and moved upstream from the river mouth at a rate equal to the distance to spawning sites divided by the number of days between spawn timing peak and run timing end.

### i. Projected temperature during migration {.tabset .tabset-pills}

**Metric:** The average of water temperatures during the upstream migration across all years of the projection period (2041-2060 or 2081-2100) estimated along the migration path from river entry to spawning sites using an upstream migration model. The model uses a moving migration window to represent the thermal exposure of CUs starting at the river mouth on the run timing start date and terminating at spawning sites on the peak spawning date. Projections from representative concentration pathways (RCP) 4.5 and 8.5 are included with an ensemble mean calculated from six global climate models.

For additional description of indicator see [A.8 Projected temperature during upstream migration (migrT)](#a.8-projected-temperature-during-upstream-migration-migrt)

```{r}
for (rcp_pick in rcp_vec)
{
  cat("#### ", rcp_pick, "\n\n", sep = "")

  filter_std <- report_dat %>%
    filter(
      rcp == rcp_pick,
      period_code == default_period
    )

  make_indicator_plots(filter_std,
    ind_pick = "migrTproj",
    make_spatial = F
  )

  cat("\n\n")
}
```

### ii. Proportional change in flow during upstream migration {.tabset .tabset-pills}

**Metric:** The proportional change in flow during the upstream migration from the baseline period (1981-2000) to the projection period (2041-2060 or 2081-2100) estimated along the migration path from river entry to spawning sites using an upstream migration model. The model uses a moving migration window to represent the average flow experienced by CUs starting at the river mouth on the run timing start date and terminating at spawning sites on the peak spawning date. Projections from representative concentration pathways (RCP) 4.5 and 8.5 are included with an ensemble mean calculated from six global climate models.

For additional description of indicator see [A.9 Proportional change in flow during upstream migration (migrQ)](#a.9-proportional-change-in-flow-during-upstream-migration-migrq)

```{r}

{
  cat("#### ", rcp_pick, "\n\n", sep = "")

  filter_std <- report_dat %>%
    filter(
      rcp == rcp_pick,
      period_code == default_period
    )

  make_indicator_plots(filter_std,
    ind_pick = "migrQpdelta",
    make_spatial = F
  )

  cat("\n\n")
}
```

### iii. Upstream migration distance {.tabset .tabset-pills}

**Metric:** The distance of the migration path from river mouth to spawning sites. For CUs with multiple spawning locations, the average of the migration distance to all spawning sites is used.

For additional description of indicator see [A.10 Upstream migration distance (migrdist)](#a.10-upstream-migration-distance-migrdist)

```{r}

```

# Nearshore Marine

#### Data Sources

**PSF CU-Specific Life History Timing** - ocean entry timing used to determine projected SST [<https://datadryad.org/dataset/doi:10.5061/dryad.wm37pvmwx>]

**SST using Quantile Delta Mapping** - CMIP6 earth system model SST values upscaled to a higher resolution using a quantile delta mapping bias correction method. Data set currently in prep for publication by ECCC (Dosser pers comm.).

**Marine Adaptive Zones** - Developed as part of CU definitions by Holtby and Ciruna (2007), adjusted to cover the marine regions.

**HOTSSea -** hindcast of the Salish Sea used for the historical climatology of SST [<https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/18/211/2025/>]. Currently used for sensitivity analysis.

**SalishSeaCast** - Regional oceanographic model of the Salish Sea used for projected SST between 2046-2065. Currently used for sensitivity analysis.

**Cumulative Impacts -** Marine habitat cumulative impacts [<https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/csas-sccs/Publications/ResDocs-DocRech/2024/2024_024-eng.html>]

#### Methods

Marine indicators represent changes to sea surface temperature and cumulative habitat impacts within marine adaptive zones surrounding the period of marine entry for each conservation unit. Sea surface temperature projections from CMIP6 models were averaged for the two months prior peak ocean entry to 2 months following peak ocean entry. Historical climatologies were estimated using the same method but averaged from the HOTSSea model for better representation of historic SSTs.

The spatial domain over which SSTs were averaged was the Strait of Georgia marine adaptive zone. The same spatial domain was applied to all CUs from the Fraser basin as they all share a common ocean entry point.

### i. Projected sea surface temperature near ocean entry {.tabset .tabset-pills}

**Metric:** The projected sea surface temperature (SST) across all years of the projection period (2041-2060 or 2081-2100) throughout the marine adaptive zone (MAZ) for the CU over a 6-month period surrounding the peak month of ocean entry. Projections from RCP 4.5 and 8.5 are included with an ensemble mean calculated from 28 global climate models.

For additional description of indicator see [A.11 Projected nearshore sea surface temperature (SSTproj)](#a.11-projected-nearshore-sea-surface-temperature-sstproj)

```{r}
for (rcp_pick in rcp_vec)
{
  cat("#### ", rcp_pick, "\n\n", sep = "")

  filter_std <- report_dat %>%
    filter(
      rcp == rcp_pick,
      period_code == default_period
    )

  make_indicator_plots(filter_std,
    ind_pick = "SSTproj",
    standardized_plots = F,
    make_spatial = F
  )

  cat("\n\n")
}
```

### ii. Rate of change in sea surface temperature near ocean entry {.tabset .tabset-pills}

**Metric:** The decadal rate of increase in SST from a baseline period to the projection period (2041-2060 or 2081-2100) throughout the marine adaptive zone (MAZ) for the CU over a 6-month period surrounding the peak month of ocean entry. Projections from RCP 4.5 and 8.5 are included with an ensemble mean calculated from 28 global climate models.

For additional description of indicator see [A.12 Rate of increase in nearshore sea surface temperatures (SSTrate)](#a.12-rate-of-increase-in-nearshore-sea-surface-temperatures-sstrate)

```{r}
for (rcp_pick in rcp_vec)
{
  cat("#### ", rcp_pick, "\n\n", sep = "")

  filter_std <- report_dat %>%
    filter(
      rcp == rcp_pick,
      period_code == default_period
    )

  make_indicator_plots(filter_std,
    ind_pick = "SSTrate",
    standardized_plots = F,
    make_spatial = F
  )

  cat("\n\n")
}
```

### iii. Cumulative impacts to nearshore marine habitat (CImpact)

**Metric:** The average cumulative impact score of nearshore habitats averaged throughout the MAZ for a CU. Cumulative impact scores are calculated for multiple habitat categories within the Pacific region including pelagic, benthic, eelgrass, and kelp forests.  Stressors included as part of the additive cumulative impact model include aquaculture, fishing, invasive species, nutrient inputs, pollution inputs, and shipping [@murray2024].

For additional description of indicator see [A.13 Cumulative impacts to nearshore marine habitat (CImpact)](#a.13-cumulative-impacts-to-nearshore-marine-habitat-cimpact)

```{r}

make_indicator_plots(report_dat,
  ind_pick = "CImpact",
  standardized_plots = F,
  make_spatial = F
)
```

# Demographics

#### Data Sources

**WSP Status Assessments** - Recent assessments for Fraser basin conservation units using methods described in CSAS 2024 [<https://www.dfo-mpo.gc.ca/csas-sccs/Publications/ScR-RS/2024/2024_004-eng.html>]

#### Methods

Demographic indicators are derived from spawner abundance data and recent Wild Salmon Policy assessments of CU status in the Fraser Basin. The CU status indicator represents the categorical status designation (Red, Amber, Green) using the Rapid Status Assessment Approach in 2022/23 [@pestal2023]. The recent generational average of spawners is derived from the same data set used to assess status and determined based on the geometric average of the number of spawners over the most recent generation with available estimates.

### i. Conservation Status

**Metric:** Recent Wild Salmon Policy (WSP) conservation status of a CU categorized as either Red, Amber, or Green. Status was assessed using the Rapid Status Assessment Approach that uses a Yes/No decision tree considering the number of recent spawners, trends in abundance, data type (absolute or relative abundance), and biological benchmarks (Pestal et al. 2023; CSAS 2024). The input data, thresholds and appropriate metrics, and final status of Fraser CUs in 2022/2023 were evaluated and agreed upon by expert judgement throughout the Rapid Status process.

For additional description of indicator see [A.14 Conservation status (CUstatus)](#a.14-conservation-status-custatus)

```{r}

make_indicator_plots(report_dat,
  ind_pick = "CUstatus",
  standardized_plots = T,
  make_spatial = F
)

cat("\n\n")
```

### ii. Recent generational average of spawners (CUnmat)

**Metric:** The geometric average of natural origin spawners (male and female) over the most recent generation with available estimates. Sockeye spawners are further refined to only include effective female spawners and not total male and female. For cyclic sockeye CUs where abundance is dominated by a single-year on the cycle line, the number of spawners from the most recent dominant year is used instead of the average over all years of a generation.

For additional description of indicator see [A.15 Recent generational average of spawners (Cunmat)](#a.15-recent-generational-average-of-spawners-cunmat)

```{r}

make_indicator_plots(report_dat,
  ind_pick = "CUnmat",
  standardized_plots = F,
  make_spatial = F
)

cat("\n\n")
```

# Genetics

#### Data Sources

**MGL Adaptive Genetic Variation Analysis** - All genetic indicator data was provided by the PBS Molecular Genetics Lab as part of a study on adaptive genetic variation of Pacific salmon (Healy et al, in prep)

#### Methods

Genetic indicators assess the genetic differences among populations to evaluate the raw material for future selection (heterozygosity) and the differences between current genetic composition and optimal genetic composition under future conditions (genomic offset). The genetic indicators described here come from a genetic analysis of Pacific salmon populations across their North American range (Healy et al, in prep), however, only populations within the Fraser basin are currently included. The analysis uses low-coverage sequencing to evaluate genome-wide variation of individuals within populations. For each population, 7-8 individuals were sequenced using samples from the DNA archive of the Pacific Biological Station Genetic Stock Identification program.

Measures of genetic diversity and genomic offset are not comparable across species, therefore, each indicator was standardized based on the range of values within a species, rather than variation across all species used for the other indicators. Genetic indicators are currently available for sockeye and Chinook salmon CUs. Coho salmon will also be added in the future.

### i. Heterozygosity

**Metric:** Heterozygosity is a common metric of genetic diversity within populations that quantifies the proportion of loci that have different alleles. Higher heterozygosity is considered indicative of greater adaptive potential to changing environmental conditions because there is more raw material upon which selection can act. Heterozygosity is measured at the individual level as the proportion of heterozygous sites, which are then averaged among all samples to get a population average value. Where multiple populations have been measured, the average across populations is taken to determine CU heterozygosity.

For additional description of indicator see [A.16 Heterozygosity (hetzyg)](#a.16-heterozygosity-hetzyg)

```{r}


make_indicator_plots(report_dat,
  ind_pick = "hetzyg",
  standardized_plots = F,
  make_spatial = F
)
```

### ii. Genomic offset

**Metric:** The genomic offset is calculated as the Euclidean distance between a population's current genetic composition and the genetic composition predicted to be optimal under future climate conditions. This distance represents the expected allele frequency change required for the population to track projected climate change, in this case based on 19 bioclim variables [<https://www.worldclim.org/data/bioclim.html>] in freshwater habitat under the RCP 8.5 scenario. Where multiple populations have been genotyped within a CU, the average genomic offset of populations was used to provide the indicator value for the CU.

For additional description of indicator see [A.17 Genomic offset (genoff)](#a.17-genomic-offset-genoff)

```{r}


make_indicator_plots(report_dat,
  ind_pick = "genoff",
  standardized_plots = F,
  make_spatial = F
)
```

# Overall Vulnerability

### Methods

Individual indicators represent one type of mechanism or trait related to climate vulnerability, however, to better understand overall vulnerability to climate change we combine standardized scores within and across indicator categories. Various methods are used in CCVAs and risk assessments for determining overall risk, such as additive or multiplicative scores, threshold approaches (Fisheries and Oceans Canada 2019), and logic models (Crozier et al. 2019), with the selection of method depending on the analytic framework and the putative mechanisms through which individual risk factors combine to determine overall risk.

For the CVIS framework, we explore four different methods that represent alternative hypotheses for how indicators and vulnerability within categories will combine to determine the overall vulnerability to climate change. Specifically, we use 1) a sum-of-averages approach that averages the values of all indicators within a category and then sums the category scores to obtain an overall vulnerability score. This gives equal weight to each category regardless of how many indicators it contains, balancing the influence of the different life stage groupings and the genetics and demographic categories. We also use 2) an average-of-all-indicators method that ignores the category type and gives all indicators an equal weighting. In addition, we use 3) a sum-of-cubic means approach that takes the cubic mean of indicator values to get a category score, then adds the category scores to determine the overall score. A cubic mean places greater weighting on high indicator values when determining category scores compared to an averaging approach. The final method is 4) a logic model that bins the standardized indicator scores into three risk categories of low, moderate, and high using fixed thresholds of 0.33 and 0.66, then determines overall vulnerability using logic rules based on the number of indicators within each category.

### Category Scores {.tabset .tabset-pills}

### Total Scores {.tabset .tabset-pills}

The following plots show total scores and CU vulnerability ranks across indicators.

```{r combined scores, fig.width=10, fig.height=8, dpi=300, out.width="100%"}
for (rcp_pick in unique(scores_tidy$rcp))
{
  cat("#### ", rcp_pick, "\n\n", sep = "")

  # Format scores_tidy to work with indicator_tile_plot
  cat_scores_as_ind <- scores_tidy %>%
    filter(
      rcp == rcp_pick, period_code == default_period,
      method == "avg", category %in% c("fwrs", "migr", "mar", "dem", "gen")
    ) %>%
    mutate(indicator = paste0("avg_", category), std_value = score)

  overall_scores_as_ind <- scores_tidy %>%
    filter(
      rcp == rcp_pick, period_code == default_period,
      method == "catavg", category == "all"
    ) %>%
    mutate(indicator = "catavg", std_value = score)

  combined_for_tile <- bind_rows(cat_scores_as_ind, overall_scores_as_ind)

  # For GCMs, default to 9 (ensemble mean)
  if ("gcm" %in% names(combined_for_tile)) {
    combined_for_tile <- combined_for_tile %>% filter(gcm == "9" | gcm == 0 | gcm == min(gcm))
  }

  p <- indicator_tile_plot(combined_for_tile,
    indicators_choose = c("avg_fwrs", "avg_migr", "avg_mar", "avg_dem", "avg_gen", "catavg"),
    overall_score_cols = "catavg",
    category_name = "Average vulnerability by category and total vulnerability"
  )

  print(p)
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

# Sensitivity Analysis

One test for the utility of an indicator is the correlation with other indicator values, and how uncertainty propagates from models into vulnerability rankings. Here we present granular uncertainty and multivariate risk profile analysis.

```{r load_sens_data, include=FALSE}
library(reshape2)
library(patchwork)
# Load new Rdata objects
load(file.path(paths$output, "sensitivity_analysis_4b_directional.Rdata"))
load(file.path(paths$output, "risk_drivers_4d.Rdata"))

# Unpack results
contributions <- sensitivity_analysis_4b_directional$contributions
mrd_stats <- sensitivity_analysis_4b_directional$mrd_stats
cor_list <- sensitivity_analysis_4b_directional$cor_matrix
categories <- sensitivity_analysis_4b_directional$categories

red_flag_summary <- risk_drivers_4d$red_flag_summary
variation_summary <- risk_drivers_4d$variation_summary
pca_output <- risk_drivers_4d$pca_output
pca_result <- risk_drivers_4d$pca_result

source_colors <- sens_source_palette
```

print(p_prop)
